title: The Complete Guide to Mortgages

seo.metaDescription: A complete guide to mortgages — how they work, the different loan types, what actually determines your rate, and what to expect from application to closing.

excerpt: A mortgage is likely the largest loan you'll ever take out — and the type, rate, and terms you choose can affect your finances for decades. Here's the complete picture, from loan types to the closing table.
intro:
A **mortgage** is a loan secured by the home you're purchasing, meaning the lender can foreclose and take the property if payments stop. In exchange for that security, mortgages carry meaningfully lower rates than unsecured debt and are repaid over long terms — commonly 15 or 30 years — that make homeownership achievable without paying the full purchase price up front.

The decisions you make around a mortgage — the loan type, the rate structure, the down payment size, whether to pay for points — compound over years and can mean tens of thousands of dollars in difference over the life of the loan. This guide covers the full picture: how mortgages work, the major loan types, what determines your rate, and what the process actually looks like from application to closing.

sections.heading: How a Mortgage Works
paragraphs: Each monthly payment is split between principal (paying down the amount borrowed) and interest (the lender's cost of lending), a structure known as amortization. Early in the loan, a much larger share of each payment goes toward interest; that ratio gradually flips as the balance shrinks, so later payments put far more toward principal.

Most mortgage payments also include property taxes and homeowners insurance, collected monthly into an escrow account and paid on your behalf when due, so the actual required payment is usually higher than principal and interest alone.

sections.heading: Fixed-Rate vs Adjustable-Rate Mortgages
paragraphs: A fixed-rate mortgage locks in the same interest rate for the entire loan term — the monthly principal-and-interest payment never changes, which makes budgeting simple and protects you if market rates rise later. An adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) typically starts with a lower introductory rate for a set period (commonly five, seven, or ten years), after which the rate adjusts periodically based on market conditions, which can raise or lower your payment.

Fixed-rate loans suit buyers planning to stay long-term or who prioritize payment certainty. ARMs can make sense for buyers confident they'll sell or refinance before the adjustable period begins, in exchange for a lower initial rate — but they carry real risk if plans change and rates rise.

sections.heading: Conventional, FHA, VA, and USDA Loans
paragraphs: A conventional loan isn't backed by a government agency and typically requires stronger credit and a larger down payment for the best terms, though options exist with down payments as low as 3%. An FHA loan is government-insured and allows lower credit scores and down payments as low as 3.5%, making it popular with first-time buyers, but requires mortgage insurance for the life of the loan in most cases. A VA loan, available to eligible veterans and service members, often requires no down payment and no mortgage insurance. A USDA loan supports buyers in eligible rural areas with no down payment required for qualifying borrowers.

sections.heading: Down Payments and Private Mortgage Insurance
paragraphs: A larger down payment reduces your loan amount, your monthly payment, and often your interest rate. On a conventional loan, putting down less than 20% typically triggers private mortgage insurance (PMI) — an added monthly cost that protects the lender, not you, and is usually cancellable once you reach 20% equity in the home.

It's rarely worth delaying a home purchase for years solely to avoid PMI if home prices and rates are rising faster than you can save — running both scenarios with a [mortgage calculator](/financial-tools/loan) usually clarifies which path actually costs less over time.

sections.heading: What Determines Your Mortgage Rate
paragraphs: Your credit score, down payment size, loan type, loan term, and debt-to-income ratio all factor into your individual rate, layered on top of broader market conditions that move rates up or down for everyone. See [mortgage interest rates](/articles/mortgage-interest-rates) for a full breakdown of how these factors interact and how much difference a stronger credit profile can make.

sections.heading: The Mortgage Application Process
paragraphs: Getting pre-approved before house hunting establishes your realistic budget and signals to sellers you're a serious buyer. Once you're under contract, the lender orders an appraisal to confirm the home's value, verifies your income and assets, and underwrites the full application before issuing final approval. The process from application to closing typically takes several weeks, and providing complete documentation promptly is the single biggest factor in keeping it on schedule.

sections.heading: Costs Beyond the Monthly Payment
paragraphs: Closing costs — lender fees, title insurance, appraisal and inspection fees, prepaid taxes and insurance — typically run a meaningful percentage of the loan amount and are due at closing, separate from the down payment. Budget for these explicitly rather than assuming the down payment is the only cash needed at the closing table, and confirm well ahead of time exactly which costs your specific lender and locality require.

keyTakeaways: Each mortgage payment splits between principal and interest, with the ratio gradually shifting toward principal as the loan matures.
Fixed-rate mortgages offer payment certainty for the full term; adjustable-rate mortgages start lower but carry rate-change risk later.
FHA, VA, and USDA loans offer lower or no down payment options for qualifying buyers compared to conventional loans.
Putting down less than 20% on a conventional loan typically triggers private mortgage insurance, an added monthly cost.
Your rate depends on credit score, down payment, loan type and term, and debt-to-income ratio, layered on top of market conditions.
Closing costs are separate from the down payment and should be budgeted for explicitly well before your closing date.

faq.question: What credit score do you need for a mortgage?
faq.answer: It varies by loan type — FHA loans can accept scores as low as the high 500s in some cases, while conventional loans typically look for a stronger score to access the best rates. Higher scores generally unlock lower rates across every loan type.

faq.question: How much down payment do I need for a house?
faq.answer: It depends on the loan type: conventional loans can go as low as 3%, FHA as low as 3.5%, and VA or USDA loans can require 0% for eligible borrowers. A larger down payment lowers your monthly payment and may avoid mortgage insurance.

faq.question: What is private mortgage insurance (PMI)?
faq.answer: An added monthly cost required on most conventional loans when the down payment is under 20%. It protects the lender if you default and can typically be cancelled once you reach 20% equity in the home.

faq.question: Is a fixed-rate or adjustable-rate mortgage better?
faq.answer: Fixed-rate suits buyers who want payment certainty and plan to stay long-term. Adjustable-rate can offer a lower initial rate for buyers confident they'll sell or refinance before the rate adjusts, but carries risk if those plans change.

faq.question: How long does it take to close on a mortgage?
faq.answer: Typically several weeks from a signed purchase agreement to closing, assuming documentation is provided promptly and the appraisal and underwriting process proceed without delays.

conclusion:
A mortgage is a decades-long financial commitment, which makes the upfront decisions — loan type, rate structure, down payment size — worth taking seriously rather than defaulting to whatever a lender first proposes. Understanding how amortization, PMI, and rate factors actually work puts you in a position to compare offers meaningfully instead of just comparing a single advertised rate.

Once you understand the mechanics here, [mortgage interest rates](/articles/mortgage-interest-rates) and [refinancing a mortgage](/articles/refinancing-a-mortgage) go into more depth on getting the best rate now and revisiting that decision later if market conditions shift in your favor.
